## 1. Students within schools

These are **synthetic observations**, not real student records. R seed 20261015
generates 250 students in 12 schools with different group sizes. Study hours are
uniform from 1 to 12; prior scores are clipped 40 + 3 × hours + normal noise with
standard deviation 8, then rounded. Assessment scores follow

$$y_i=50+1.8\,\mathrm{hours}_i+0.2\,\mathrm{prior}_i+b_{g(i)}+\epsilon_i,
\quad b_g\sim N(0,6^2),\quad\epsilon_i\sim N(0,5^2).$$

The school effect is shared by students in that school. Conditional on school
effects, residual errors are independent. Integrating over those effects makes
students within the same school correlated. Scores are continuous, unlike the
binary outcomes in logistic/probit or counts in Poisson. Known simulation
parameters and estimated parameters are different objects.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.stats import norm
from IPython.display import Math, display
ROOT=next(p for p in [Path.cwd(),*Path.cwd().parents] if (p/'Cargo.toml').exists())
import sys
sys.path.insert(0,str(ROOT/'docs/figures'))
from bridge import render_figure
observations=pd.read_csv(ROOT/'docs/data/schools.csv')
X=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(observations)),observations[['study_hours','prior_score']]])
y=observations.score.to_numpy()
labels=list(dict.fromkeys(observations.school))
groups=pd.Categorical(observations.school,categories=labels).codes
members=[np.flatnonzero(groups==g) for g in range(len(labels))]
n,p=X.shape;G=len(members)
fixture=json.loads((ROOT/'tests/fixtures/lmm-r.json').read_text())['cases'][0]
np.testing.assert_array_equal(X,fixture['x']);np.testing.assert_array_equal(y,fixture['y'])
display(observations.head(8))
display(observations[['study_hours','prior_score','score']].corr())
def number(value):
    text = f"{value:.6g}"
    if "e" in text:
        mantissa, exponent = text.split("e")
        return mantissa + rf"\times10^{{{int(exponent)}}}"
    return text

def show_matrix(symbol, values, limit=6):
    matrix = np.asarray(values)
    if matrix.ndim == 1:
        matrix = matrix[:, None]
    indices = list(range(len(matrix))) if len(matrix) <= limit else [0,1,2,None,len(matrix)-1]
    columns = list(range(matrix.shape[1])) if matrix.shape[1] <= limit else [0,1,2,None,matrix.shape[1]-1]
    rows = [" & ".join(r"\ddots" if j is None else r"\vdots" for j in columns) if i is None
            else " & ".join(r"\cdots" if j is None else number(matrix[i,j]) for j in columns) for i in indices]
    display(Math(symbol + r"=\begin{bmatrix}" + r" \\ ".join(rows)
                 + r"\end{bmatrix}" + rf"\quad({matrix.shape[0]}\times{matrix.shape[1]})"))

def show_dot(symbol, left, right):
    terms = [rf"({number(a)})\cdot({number(b)})" for a,b in zip(left,right)]
    if len(terms) > 3:
        terms = terms[:2] + [r"\cdots", terms[-1]]
    display(Math(symbol + "=" + "+".join(terms) + r"\approx" + number(np.asarray(left) @ right)))


show_matrix('X',X);show_matrix('y',y)
Z=np.eye(G)[groups]
show_matrix('Z',Z)
print('Observations:',n,'Fixed coefficients:',p,'Schools:',G)
```

X and y are observed inputs; ones are a constructed fixed-intercept column.
Z is a constructed group-indicator matrix: each row has exactly one 1. Group
labels identify membership; they are not numeric predictors. Matrix displays
truncate rows/columns using dots while calculations use every observation.
Sample correlations alone do not establish causation.

## 2. Conditional and marginal models

The conditional model is

$$y\mid b\sim N(X\beta+Zb,\sigma^2 I),\qquad b\sim N(0,\tau^2 I_G).$$

Fixed effects beta describe the population relationship. Random intercepts b
are modeled as draws from a common zero-mean distribution, not G freely estimated
fixed coefficients. sigma² is within-school residual variance; tau² is between-school
variance after accounting for X. Normality and independence are modeling assumptions.

Marginalizing over b gives

$$y\sim N(X\beta,V),\qquad V=\sigma^2 I+\tau^2 ZZ^\top.$$

For two different students in the same school, covariance is tau². For different
schools it is zero. A single student's marginal residual variance is sigma² + tau².
The **intraclass correlation**, conditional on fixed predictors, is

$$\mathrm{ICC}=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2}.$$

This is not the raw Pearson correlation of the observed scores. The covariance
structure concerns unexplained variation after accounting for fixed effects.
For a school of size m,

$$V_g=\sigma^2 I_m+\tau^2\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top.$$

```{python}
# Display a block using generating variances, not fitted or starting parameters.
m=len(members[0]);Vg=25*np.eye(m)+36*np.ones((m,m))
show_matrix(r'V_{\mathrm{school\ 1}}\text{ at generating parameters}',Vg)
print('Generating ICC:',36/(36+25))
```

## 3. The likelihood integrates out group effects

The marginal Gaussian log-likelihood is

$$\ell(\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2)=-\frac12\left[
 n\log(2\pi)+\log|V|+(y-X\beta)^\top V^{-1}(y-X\beta)\right].$$

This is not a Gaussian likelihood using conditional residuals as independent
observations, and not the joint likelihood obtained by treating b as ordinary
fixed parameters. It includes the covariance determinant and integrates over b.

For fixed variance components, maximizing over beta gives **generalized least
squares (GLS)**:

$$X^\top V^{-1}X\hat\beta=X^\top V^{-1}y.$$

OLS assumes covariance proportional to I. GLS changes how residual directions
are weighted because group means and within-group deviations have different variances.
The production solve uses whitening and SVD, rather than inverting this cross-product.

## 4. Whiten groups instead of building a huge matrix

Write rho=tau²/sigma² and C=I+rho ZZ'. For one group,

$$C_g=I_m+\rho\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top,\quad
C_g^{-1}=I_m-\frac{\rho}{1+m\rho}\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top,\quad
\log|C_g|=\log(1+m\rho).$$

The group-mean direction has eigenvalue 1+m rho; all m-1 directions orthogonal
to it have eigenvalue 1. Whitening preserves within-group deviations and divides
the mean by sqrt(1+m rho):

$$C_g^{-1/2}v=(v-\bar v\mathbf1)+\frac{\bar v}{\sqrt{1+m\rho}}\mathbf1.$$

This transformation applies to y and each column of X. The squared whitened
residual norm is q=(y-X beta)' C^-1 (y-X beta). It requires storage linear in n,
without constructing the full n × n V. Scaling X's columns as D gives A=XD^-1;
weighted SVD solves C^-1/2 A theta approximately C^-1/2 y, with beta=D^-1 theta.

```{python}
scales=np.linalg.norm(X,axis=0);A=X/scales

def whiten(values,rho):
    matrix=np.asarray(values)
    if matrix.ndim==1:matrix=matrix[:,None]
    output=matrix.copy()
    for indices in members:
        mean=matrix[indices].mean(axis=0)
        output[indices]=(matrix[indices]-mean)+mean/np.sqrt(1+len(indices)*rho)
    return output

rho_trial=1.0
show_matrix(r'C_{g}^{-1}\text{ at trial }\rho=1',np.eye(m)-np.ones((m,m))/(1+m))
show_matrix(r'C^{-1/2}X\text{ at trial }\rho=1',whiten(X,rho_trial))
show_matrix(r'C^{-1/2}y\text{ at trial }\rho=1',whiten(y,rho_trial))
wx=whiten(X,rho_trial);wy=whiten(y,rho_trial)[:,0]
show_dot(r'(X^\top C^{-1}y)_2',wx[:,1],wy)
show_matrix(r'X^\top C^{-1}X\text{ for illustration}',wx.T@wx)
```

Trial rho is a starting/example variance ratio, not an observed predictor or a
known generating parameter. The cross-product shown is for understanding the dot
products; production estimation uses the SVD of an equivalent compact weighted
design, derived next.

### Cache a square-root reduction, following the lme4 idea

lme4 evaluates a **penalized least-squares** problem and eliminates the random
coefficients through a block factorization. For our single random intercept,
the same elimination has a particularly simple form. At positive rho,

$$\min_b\left\{\sum_{i\in g}(r_i-b)^2+\frac{b^2}{\rho}\right\}
=\sum_{i\in g}(r_i-\bar r_g)^2+\frac{m_g\bar r_g^2}{1+m_g\rho}.$$

The minimizer is $b=m_g\rho\bar r_g/(1+m_g\rho)$; substitute it into the
left side to obtain the right side. At rho=0 the limiting solution has b=0.
Within-group deviations have weight 1; only the group-mean weight changes
with the variance ratio. This is the link between penalized least squares
and the marginal GLS residual norm above.

We can therefore do most observation-level work **once**. Let W contain
within-group-centered rows of the augmented matrix $[A\;y]$, and let row g of
M be $\sqrt{m_g}[\bar A_g\;\bar y_g]$. Take a thin QR factorization $W=Q_wR_w$.
Since $Q_w^\top Q_w=I$, for any coefficient vector theta,

$$q(\rho,\theta)=\left\|W\begin{bmatrix}-\theta\\1\end{bmatrix}\right\|^2
+\sum_g\frac{\left(M_g\begin{bmatrix}-\theta\\1\end{bmatrix}\right)^2}{1+m_g\rho}
=\left\|K(\rho)\begin{bmatrix}-\theta\\1\end{bmatrix}\right\|^2,$$

$$K(\rho)=\begin{bmatrix}R_w\\
\operatorname{diag}\{(1+m_g\rho)^{-1/2}\}M\end{bmatrix}.$$

K has only p+1+G rows. The fixed intercept's centered column is zero; that
poses no problem for QR of the augmented matrix. Full rank is checked on the
complete weighted fixed design, including the group-mean rows.

```{python}
augmented=np.column_stack([A,y])
centered=augmented.copy();means=[];sizes=np.array([len(rows) for rows in members])
for rows in members:
    mean=augmented[rows].mean(axis=0)
    centered[rows]=augmented[rows]-mean
    means.append(np.sqrt(len(rows))*mean)
means=np.asarray(means)
_,within_R=np.linalg.qr(centered,mode='reduced')
compact=np.vstack([within_R,means/np.sqrt(1+sizes[:,None]*rho_trial)])
show_matrix(r'R_w',within_R)
show_matrix(r'K(\rho=1)',compact)
trial_theta=np.array([40.,1.,.1])*scales
contrast=np.r_[-trial_theta,1.]
compressed_q=np.linalg.norm(compact@contrast)**2
full_q=np.linalg.norm(whiten(y-X@(trial_theta/scales),rho_trial))**2
np.testing.assert_allclose(compressed_q,full_q,atol=1e-8,rtol=1e-12)
print('Original rows:',n,'Compact rows:',len(compact))
print('Trial residual norm squared: full =',full_q,'compact =',compressed_q)
compressed_beta=np.linalg.lstsq(compact[:,:p],compact[:,p],rcond=None)[0]/scales
full_beta=np.linalg.lstsq(whiten(A,rho_trial),whiten(y,rho_trial)[:,0],rcond=None)[0]/scales
np.testing.assert_allclose(compressed_beta,full_beta,atol=1e-9,rtol=1e-10)
show_matrix(r'\hat\beta(\rho=1)\text{ from compact solve}',compressed_beta)
```

Production caches R_w and M once, then uses SVD on the compact weighted fixed
design. Covariance is computed only at the selected fit. The later Python
profile deliberately uses the full whitening formulation as an independent
check of the same mathematics. For a million observations and 100 groups with
three coefficients, each trial now factors 104 rows instead of a million.

This borrows **elimination and reuse** from lme4; it does not copy lme4 source
code or introduce its sparse Cholesky/CHOLMOD backend. Using QR/SVD square roots
also avoids subtracting nearly equal Gram matrices or forming a residual norm
as $y^\top y-\hat\beta^\top X^\top y$. That preserves accuracy with correlated
predictors and small residual variation. See
[lme4's PLS versus GLS derivation](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/articles/PLSvGLS.pdf)
and the [measured optimization](../benchmarks/lmm.qmd#native-rust-optimization).

## 5. Profile out beta and sigma²; optimize one variance ratio

At fixed rho, GLS finds beta and q. The ML scale estimate is

$$\hat\sigma^2(\rho)=q(\rho)/n,\qquad\hat\tau^2=\rho\hat\sigma^2.$$

Substitution gives the profiled **negative** log-likelihood

$$f(\rho)=\frac12\left[n\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(q/n)\}
+\sum_g\log(1+m_g\rho)\right].$$

A lower value is better. No generic multivariate optimizer is required for this
particular random-intercept model. For GLS residuals r=y-X beta, the envelope theorem
lets us differentiate the optimized objective without differentiating beta:

$$q'(\rho)=-\sum_g\frac{(\sum_{i\in g}r_i)^2}{(1+m_g\rho)^2},\qquad
f'(\rho)=\frac12\left[n\frac{q'}q+\sum_g\frac{m_g}{1+m_g\rho}\right].$$

Rust searches t=log(1+rho) on a 0.5-spaced grid from 0 to 32, then refines every
negative-to-positive derivative crossing by 40 bisections. The derivative with
respect to t is (1+rho)f'(rho). It compares those candidates with rho=0 exactly,
and rejects an optimum beyond the upper bound. The finite grid can miss unusually
narrow unbracketed stationary points: this initial search is not an exhaustive
global-optimum guarantee. The Python walkthrough independently brackets roots of
the same score, using SciPy's root solver.

```{python}
def profile(t):
    rho=np.expm1(t);wx=whiten(A,rho);wy=whiten(y,rho)[:,0]
    U,s,Vt=np.linalg.svd(wx,full_matrices=False)
    beta=(Vt.T@((U.T@wy)/s))/scales
    residual=y-X@beta
    q=np.sum(whiten(residual,rho)**2);variance=q/n
    logdet=sum(np.log1p(len(indices)*rho) for indices in members)
    objective=.5*(n*(np.log(2*np.pi)+1+np.log(variance))+logdet)
    qprime=-sum((residual[indices].sum()/(1+len(indices)*rho))**2 for indices in members)
    derivative=.5*(1+rho)*(n*qprime/q+sum(len(indices)/(1+len(indices)*rho) for indices in members))
    return dict(rho=rho,beta=beta,variance=variance,objective=objective,derivative=derivative,s=s,Vt=Vt)

grid=np.arange(0,32.5,.5);values=[profile(t) for t in grid];candidates=[0.]
for left,right,a,b in zip(grid[:-1],grid[1:],values[:-1],values[1:]):
    if a['derivative']<0 and b['derivative']>=0:
        candidates.append(brentq(lambda t:profile(t)['derivative'],left,right,xtol=1e-12))
best_t=min(candidates,key=lambda t:profile(t)['objective'])
fit=profile(best_t);rho=fit['rho'];beta=fit['beta'];variance=fit['variance'];tau=rho*variance
print('Candidate log ratios:',candidates)
print('Residual variance:',variance,'Group variance:',tau,'ICC:',rho/(1+rho))
show_matrix(r'\hat\beta',beta)

curve=np.linspace(0,4,81);objective=np.array([profile(t)['objective'] for t in curve])
render_figure('profile',dict(curve=curve.tolist(),objective=(objective-objective.min()).tolist(),
                           best_t=float(best_t),boundary=float(profile(0)['objective']-objective.min())))
```

ML is **not REML**. Restricted maximum likelihood adjusts for estimating fixed
coefficients and adds a fixed-design determinant term; it often improves variance
estimation with limited groups. R lmer defaults to REML, so all comparisons here
explicitly set REML=FALSE. No RSS/(n-p) correction is substituted for the ML scale.

## 6. Shrinkage: estimate each school's intercept

At the fitted variances, the Gaussian conditional mean of a group effect is

$$\hat b_g=\frac{m_g\hat\tau^2}{\hat\sigma^2+m_g\hat\tau^2}\bar r_g,
\qquad\bar r_g=\frac1{m_g}\sum_{i\in g}(y_i-x_i^\top\hat\beta).$$

To derive it, combine the prior term b²/tau² with the within-group likelihood
sum(r_i-b)²/sigma². The resulting quadratic in b has precision
1/tau² + m/sigma² and linear term sum r_i/sigma², yielding this conditional mean.
The multiplier lies between 0 and 1: noisy/small groups shrink more toward zero.
These empirical BLUPs use fitted variances; they are not known realized effects.
At tau²=0 all group effects are zero.

```{python}
fixed_fitted=X@beta;marginal_residuals=y-fixed_fitted
random_effects=np.array([(len(indices)*rho/(1+len(indices)*rho))*marginal_residuals[indices].mean() for indices in members])
fitted=fixed_fitted+random_effects[groups];residuals=y-fitted
summary=pd.DataFrame({'school':labels,'n':[len(i) for i in members],
                     'raw residual mean':[marginal_residuals[i].mean() for i in members],
                     'shrinkage':[len(i)*rho/(1+len(i)*rho) for i in members],
                     'estimated random intercept':random_effects})
display(summary)
show_dot(r'x_1^\top\hat\beta',X[0],beta)
display(pd.DataFrame({'observed':y,'population fit':fixed_fitted,'conditional fit':fitted,
                      'marginal residual':marginal_residuals,'conditional residual':residuals}).head(8))
```

The population fit describes a group with mean effect zero. The conditional fit
uses this sample's estimated group effect. It is not a held-out predictive result:
the same outcomes helped estimate those effects. There is no new-group prediction API.

## 7. Fixed-effect uncertainty and model statistics

The plug-in GLS covariance is

$$\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=(X^\top\hat V^{-1}X)^{-1}
=\hat\sigma^2 D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1},$$

where V and S on the right are the SVD factors of the whitened scaled design
(the SVD factor V is distinct from the observation covariance V). Standard errors
are diagonal square roots. We report asymptotic normal Wald z-tests and intervals.
There is no exact OLS t distribution, Satterthwaite/Kenward–Roger adjustment or
variance-component p-value. With only twelve groups, normal inference should be
read cautiously: many students do not substitute for many independent groups.

AIC uses p+2 parameters: fixed coefficients and both variance components, counting
them even when tau²=0. Group BLUPs are not counted as G additional free parameters.
The returned df_residual=n-p is informational, not a t-test denominator.

```{python}
s=fit['s'];Vt=fit['Vt']
covariance=variance*((Vt.T/s)@(Vt/s[:,None]))/scales[:,None]/scales[None,:]
se=np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance));z=beta/se;p_values=2*norm.sf(abs(z))
conf_int=np.column_stack([beta-norm.ppf(.975)*se,beta+norm.ppf(.975)*se])
display(pd.DataFrame({'estimate':beta,'SE':se,'z':z,'p':p_values,'95% lower':conf_int[:,0],'95% upper':conf_int[:,1]},index=['intercept','study hours','prior score']))
calculated=dict(coefficients=beta,covariance=covariance,std_errors=se,z_statistics=z,p_values=p_values,conf_int=conf_int,
 fixed_fitted=fixed_fitted,fitted=fitted,residuals=residuals,marginal_residuals=marginal_residuals,random_effects=random_effects,
 residual_variance=variance,random_intercept_variance=tau,sigma=np.sqrt(variance),icc=rho/(1+rho),
 log_likelihood=-fit['objective'],aic=2*(p+2)+2*fit['objective'],df_residual=n-p)
for key,value in calculated.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value,fixture['reference']['result'][key],atol=1e-7,rtol=1e-6,err_msg=key)
print('Every statistical field agrees with the saved lme4 ML fixture.')
```

## 8. Boundaries, assumptions and experiments

A zero random-intercept variance is a valid boundary ML fit. It gives OLS fixed
coefficients but uses the ML scale RSS/n for standard errors, rather than OLS's
unbiased RSS/(n-p). Positive residual variance is required; numerically perfect
fits and unsupported zero-residual-variance limits fail. One group or all-singleton
data are rejected because the two variances cannot be separately identified under
this first contract; singleton groups are allowed when other groups repeat.

Assumptions include independent groups, Gaussian random intercepts independent
of X, homoskedastic Gaussian residuals and the supplied linear fixed mean. Ignoring
correlation between random effects and predictors can bias fixed effects. The first
implementation has one grouping factor, no random slopes or REML. Missing rows in
x, y or groups are deleted together, with warnings and row metadata.

Try merging all groups into one; assigning each row a new group; removing the
school variation in the simulation; or increasing residual noise. Which makes the
model unidentified, pushes group variance to zero, or increases shrinkage?

## Rust connections

`fit_random_intercept` owns numeric vectors and usize group IDs. A HashMap assigns
first-appearance group indices; vectors of member row positions make group means
and group means explicit. ProfileData caches a QR square-root summary and group
means; a private Profile struct holds one variance-ratio evaluation. nalgebra's
SVD handles compact GLS and final covariance; the dedicated scalar
search remains visible in `crates/stats-core/src/mixed.rs`. Result/`?` propagates
validation and numerical errors. The binding preserves typed PHP group labels,
handles missing rows and converts the complete result to ordinary arrays.

See the [PHP contract](../reference-models.qmd#gaussian-random-intercept-mixed-model),
[executed comparison](lmm-verification.qmd),
[lme4 lmer reference](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/lmer.html), and
[statsmodels MixedLM](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/mixed_linear.html).
